content.text: I want you to conduct deep evidence-based investigation & research to come up with the best positional sizing and risk management practice for bolt-v2. I have positional sizer, which is a wrong name, which essentially is a kill switch and loss manager. we should have a respective issue or epic around it.

I’m treating this as a read-only architecture and evidence investigation. I’ll use the Superpowers workflow for framing, targeted codebase navigation to trace the current “positional sizer,” and the planning workflow to turn the findings into a concrete issue/epic recommendation; I’ll also inspect the repository’s tracker before proposing anything new.
this should be read only and planning and spec session

Understood: strictly read-only. I won’t edit files, create tracker items, commit, push, or open a PR. The deliverable will be an evidence-backed architecture recommendation plus a proposed spec/issue structure in chat, grounded in the current code and existing tracker state.
you should conduct internal adverserial reviews to have a clear confidence in the architecture

I’ll add multiple independent adversarial passes over the recommendation—portfolio-loss containment, execution/admission boundaries, statistical sizing assumptions, and operational fail-closed behavior—and report disagreements, residual risks, and confidence limits. I’m keeping those reviews internal to this read-only session; I won’t invoke external reviewers or mutate the repository. The SpecKit file-writing workflow is intentionally out of scope because you required read-only work.

Initial context: this checkout is on `vorflux/strategy-agnostic-substrate`, and it already contains an unrelated uncommitted edit in `src/bolt_v3_outcome_groups.rs`; I’ll leave it untouched. Beads produced no project context, so I’m checking whether durable tracking is actually GitHub-based before treating either system as authoritative.
we should checkout main and start from there

I’ll base the investigation on current `main` while preserving the unrelated uncommitted edit. I’m using the worktree-isolation workflow here because switching this dirty checkout directly could carry or obstruct that change; I’ll first determine whether a clean `main` worktree already exists.

The investigation is now anchored to a clean isolated checkout of verified current `main` at `30119eb4c` (local `main`, `origin/main`, and remote `refs/heads/main` all matched). The original checkout and its uncommitted edit remain untouched. I’m skipping build/setup because this is read-only research and the repository forbids compile-heavy local Rust verification by default.

I’m now tracing four evidence layers on `main`: the current runtime path, configuration and fail-closed tests, design/spec history, and existing GitHub issue ownership. I’ll separate what the code actually enforces today from names or docs that merely suggest behavior.

A material finding is already emerging: `main` has completed the rename to `capital_admission`, and its own spec explicitly says the old component was an authorize/reserve/reject gate, not a size chooser. A separate real sizing engine is tracked as #712, while the atomic multi-dimensional risk ledger is split to #973—but the #712 spec referenced by #973 is not present on current `main`. I’m checking the live GitHub issues before deciding whether this is missing accepted scope, superseded design, or simply issue-owned work not yet merged.

One scope question while I continue: what loss tolerance should this architecture treat as non-negotiable—expressed as a maximum account drawdown, a maximum probability of ruin, or both? Until you answer, I’ll assume “survival first”: maximize conservative long-run growth only inside explicit drawdown and ruin bounds, never optimize raw expected profit alone.

The code/tracker evidence points to three distinct controls that should not be conflated: a sizing advisor, an atomic pre-trade risk-budget gate, and a reactive loss/kill controller. I’m now testing that separation against primary academic work, official venue mechanics, and formal algorithmic-trading control standards before recommending issue boundaries.
